1:
What this basket was, and how it differed from the other firstfruits of the calendar, is settled first. Henry distinguishes it from the sheaf offered for the whole land after the passover, this being the private offering each man brought at the feast of firstfruits; and he describes the practice — going into the field as the fruits ripened, marking what was most forward, and laying it by, so that wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates went into one basket with leaves between them. Gill separates it from three other offerings at once — the barley sheaf, the two wave loaves at wheat harvest, and the cake of the dough — and adds on rabbinic authority that only seven kinds were owed. Wesley makes it the duty of each master of a family, either on first settling or once a year at one of the three feasts. Keil handles the one grammatical point bearing on quantity: the word is partitive, a portion of the first of the fruit — from which, he insists against Schultz, it does not follow that the firstfruits were not all delivered at the sanctuary, only that not all had to be put in a basket and set down there.

On why it was commanded, Calvin gives the fullest answer and ties it to another payment. The firstfruits were required for the same reason as the tribute for every soul, that they might confess that they and all they had belonged to God; but where the tribute symbolised their emancipation, the firstfruits testified that the land itself was tributary, and that they held it by no better title than tenants at will, the sovereignty remaining with God alone. So the rite renewed yearly the recollection of their adoption: they were fed not promiscuously, like the Gentiles, but like children, their food therefore sacred. He adds that the typical rite has ceased while its true observation remains, since whether we eat or drink we are to do all to the glory of God. Clarke reaches a similar end more briefly: the offering was to keep them in continual remembrance of God's kindness in preserving them and fulfilling his promises, the firstfruits consecrated to the author of every good and perfect gift.

Henry turns the law into three lessons, and the middle one is the sharpest. First, to acknowledge God as the giver of what supports natural life. Second, to deny ourselves, since what is first ripe is what we are fondest of — my soul desired the firstripe fruit — so that laying it by taught them to prefer the glorifying of his name to the gratifying of their appetite. Third, to give God the first and best, as those who believe him the first and best of beings; which he applies to those who consecrate the days of their youth.

The two remaining details belong to the priest. Gill reports that he waved the basket with his hand under the owner's, moving it toward the corners of the earth in acknowledgment that the Lord owns the whole; and on the phrase the priest that shall be in those days he passes on the Targum's reading that the high priest is meant, and the inference that the law binds only while there is one — before turning it to Christ, by whom we offer the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of our lips. Calvin, reading forward into the words the offerer had to say, notes that they confess the land was gained neither by their own strength nor by good fortune but by free gift according to promise, and that they date themselves not from Abraham but from Jacob, in whose person the grace of God shone out more brightly.
5:
Four words at the head of the confession have been rendered six different ways, and Clarke lays the versions out side by side. The Vulgate has a Syrian persecuted my father; the Septuagint, my father abandoned Syria; the Targum, Laban the Syrian endeavoured to destroy my father; the Syriac, my father was led out of Syria into Egypt; the Arabic, that Laban had almost destroyed him; and Houbigant, dissenting from all, famine oppressed my father, who went down into Egypt — got by detaching a letter from the word for Aramaean and finding the sense of famine in the Arabic cognate. Clarke judges that the Syrian is Jacob, so called from his long residence in Syria with his father-in-law, and that his being ready to perish refers to the hard usage and severe labour of that service, which impaired his health and often put his life in danger. Keil settles the same crux more shortly and in the same direction: the phrase is a lost, a perishing Aramaean was my father, and not, as the Chaldee, the Arabic and Luther render it, that the Aramaean Laban sought to destroy him. Wesley takes the epithet as true on three counts at once — Jacob was a Syrian by origin, since Abraham and Rebekah came from Mesopotamia, by education, and by his relations, his wives being Syrian and his children so by their mother — and leaves the peril open between poverty and the rage of Esau and the treachery of Laban.

The rest of the confession draws only brief notes, most of them Gill's: that the offerer was to lift up his voice, or, on another reading, to answer the priest's question, what is this thou hast brought; that the evil entreatment was the two edicts, that the midwives should kill the male children and that the people should drown them; and that the bringing to this place came only after forty years in the wilderness.

One point of ceremony is disputed. At verse 10 the offerer is again told to set the basket down, though the priest has already set it down at verse 4. Keil reports that some read this as implying the offerer held it throughout the prayer, in direct opposition to the earlier verses, and rejects it: the words simply close the instructions. He is equally firm about its setting: the rejoicing points to the sacrificial meal that followed the act of worship, and the presentation was made on the pilgrimages at the three yearly festivals, against the attempt to restrict the words to meals prepared from the tithes.

On the command to rejoice the two Methodists are of one mind and press it hard. Clarke says God intends his followers to be happy, and to eat their bread with gladness and singleness of heart; those who eat their meat grudgingly, under pretence of their own unworthiness, profane God's bounties and shall have no thanks for their voluntary humility. He then turns the two named guests into a charge: the Levite has no inheritance, let him rejoice with thee; the stranger has no home, let him feel thee to be his friend and his father. Wesley makes the same point from the other end: a man takes comfort in all his employments once he has sanctified them by giving God his portion, and it is God's will we be cheerful not only in attending his ordinances but in enjoying the gifts of his providence, tracing the streams up to the fountain. Gill, characteristically, glosses the good things as all the blessings of goodness and mercies of life which God in his kind providence had favoured them with.
12:
The tithe here is the one laid down two chapters earlier, and they agree on what changed in the third year. Henry says the second tithe, spent in the other two years at the feasts, was in the third year spent at home entertaining the poor; Wesley adds the widening of the guest list, from owners and Levites at Jerusalem to strangers, fatherless and widows in their own dwellings; Clarke notes that by the letter the tithe was for the Levites, drawn once in three years.

Where the declaration was made is disputed, three to one. Gill says it was not made in the tabernacle or temple at all, since the tithe was eaten in the owner's own gates; Wesley calls it a private address, solemn but at home; Keil states flatly that saying before the Lord does not here denote prayer in the sanctuary. Henry alone puts it at the sanctuary: at the next feast they were to testify as upon oath that they had been true to their trust — which he grounds on this tithe being disposed of out of sight of the priests, so that great confidence was reposed in the people's honesty. Keil explains why a prayer is prescribed for this tithe and no other: it was consumed throughout the land in meals for the poor, so the requirement would not follow by analogy from the firstfruits, as where the meal was eaten at the sanctuary.

Calvin is exercised by the form of the protestation. Moses stimulates them, he says, by setting God before their eyes as if the tithes were paid into his hand, nothing awakening men more than when God is produced as their judge; the speaker condemns himself if he has defrauded, and prays for grace if not. But the claim not to have transgressed or forgotten must be referred to the matter in hand only: it would be temerity and arrogance to boast of having kept the law in every part, and the words signify desire rather than perfection, the full purpose of the mind to obey. Henry draws the parallel: we are no longer under such appropriations of our revenue, but we are commanded to give alms, and then, and not otherwise, all things are clean to us; and the clause about forgetting forecloses the excuse that the commandment slipped the mind.

The denials of verse 14 are read four ways between them. On eating in mourning, Gill and Keil take it of mourning for the dead, which left a man legally unclean while the body lay unburied. Calvin reports the almost universal exposition, that want might have tempted them to fraud and they assert that even in poverty they kept their hands off the hallowed things — while allowing that the word might mean the anxiety of a guilty mind, so that the hot iron of an evil conscience should burn the eater. Wesley alone takes it of grudging rather than grief: not eaten in sorrow at giving away so much of one's profits, but cheerfully feasted with the poor as commanded. On giving to the dead, Clarke reads idolatry, an idol being generally a dead man whom ignorance had deified, and compares the flesh offered to idols and sold in the shambles; Wesley reads funeral feasting, provisions being sent to the relations of the deceased so that both guests and food were legally polluted, a double fault; Calvin follows the funeral reading but objects that it is unclear why such a denial should be needed.

The closing petition draws one remarkable inference. Calvin observes that they are told to bless a land already flowing with milk and honey, and concludes it was not fertile by nature but because God daily watered it by his secret blessing. Wesley takes the order of profession and prayer as showing how vain the prayers of the disobedient are.
16:
The words this day are glossed carefully. Gill takes them for Moses' own, covering everything repeated in the book: he had been several days about it, but this being the last day, all of it is said to be commanded that day — with the rabbinic turn added that every day was to be reckoned new, as if the laws had been given that morning. Henry draws two enforcements. First, these are God's commands, not the dictates of Moses' own wisdom: do them and not dispute them, do them and not draw back, and not carelessly but with the whole heart. Second, the covenant binds both ways — Israel had avouched God implicitly by attending on his word and expressly at Sinai — so that we forswear ourselves if, having taken the Lord for our God, we do not make conscience of obeying him.

Calvin presses the same demand and then defends it. God is the author of the Law, and since it was delivered specially to this people its observation is the more enjoined on them; by so often calling them to obedience he indirectly rebukes their indifference, men growing careless unless often stirred up. With all thy soul means serious apprehension free of disguise, nothing being more displeasing to God than hypocrisy. But is it not vain to demand what no mortal can perform? The whole heart, he answers, is set against a divided one and means an undeceitful heart; and it is not absurd to propose to believers an object they aim at though the flesh keeps them from it. It is the move he made at the protestation a few verses earlier, where the claim to have kept the commandments was read as desire rather than perfection.

Keil finds two things in the mutual avouching: Israel's acceptance of the laws was a practical declaration that it would take Jehovah as its God, and the Lord's giving of them a confirmation of his promise that Israel should be his treasured people of possession. His rendering of the verb is unusual and the others do not follow it: not that Israel avouched, but that Israel let the Lord say it, giving him occasion to call himself their God. Clarke, Wesley and Gill keep the plainer sense of a public declaration, Clarke adding that God avouched on his side by the blessings he pours down, so ratifying the covenant.

What the promised exaltation amounts to is the real dispute, and four answers appear. Gill keeps it comparative: other nations were famous for extent and wealth, but Israel stood higher for having the Lord as King and such laws — the end being to make them not merely high but holy. Keil turns the three words about, so that Israel becomes an object of praise and renown not of itself but of the God who made it; the sanctifying of the people was the design and end of its election. Calvin makes it reciprocal and then hides it: nothing is more honourable to us than to give God his due honour, and he desires to be glorified by us in no other way than by making us partakers of his glory — but this excellency of the Church, though it shines in the world, is hidden from the blind, being spiritual and praised only before God and the angels. Clarke goes the opposite way, into national politics. Righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people: Israel was greatest while it kept the testimonies and most contemptible when it forsook them — and he turns from the text to address his own country, that neither fleets nor armies can secure permanence among the nations, but righteousness alone. And the confession, he adds, made men brought into affluence acknowledge their former wretchedness publicly, since one who rises from poverty and forgets it grows proud and oppressive.
